Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

dedicate verb

a book, a building or a work to someone

also dedication (of a book), dedicated to

classical

Cic. ND 3.13 (Lewis & Short)
Phaedr. 3 prol. 30; Plin. NH praef. 12; Quint. 4 prooem. 4 (Lewis & Short)

dēdicō, dēdicāre, dēdicāvī, dēdicātum

verb, first conjugation

Classically of temples, altars and statues, given to a god; of a book inscribed to a person, from Phaedrus and the elder Pliny on (Lewis & Short). To dedicate oneself to a task is another word (see commitment, devote).

Other words

  • dicō, dicāre, dicāvī, dicātum — dedicate, consecrate

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Liv. 1.7: āra condita atque dicāta (Lewis & Short)

    The simple verb, chiefly of things given to the gods; not the common verb dīcō, “say”, which has a long ī.

  • librum ad aliquem mittere — dedicate a book to someone

    also used · classical · Cic. Att. 8.11.7; Div. 2.3 (Lewis & Short, s.v. dēdicō)

    Cicero’s way: a book is “sent to” the person it honours (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • nōnne ab A. Postumiō aedem Castorī ac Pollūcī in forō dēdicātam vidēs?

    don’t you see the temple in the forum that Aulus Postumius dedicated to Castor and Pollux?Cic. ND 3.13 (Lewis & Short)

  • perfectō operis tibi dēdicātī tertiō librō

    when I had finished the third book of the work dedicated to youQuint. 4 prooem. 4 (Lewis & Short)

See also commitment, book.

SourcesLewis & Short: dedico · Lewis & Short: dico
